answer_text:
We want

\[
\limsup_{j\to\infty} a_j
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
a_j = |\sin j|^{\sin j}.
\]

We take \(j\) in radians. For \(j\ge 1\), \(\sin j\neq 0\) because \(\pi\) is irrational, so the expression is well-defined.

---

### 1. Use the density of \(\{\sin j\}\)

Since \(1/(2\pi)\) is irrational, the sequence

\[
j \pmod{2\pi}
\]

is dense in \([0,2\pi]\). Therefore

\[
\{\sin j : j\in \mathbb N\}
\]

is dense in \([-1,1]\). In fact, every tail of the sequence is dense, so we can find integers \(j\to\infty\) with \(\sin j\) arbitrarily close to any prescribed value in \([-1,1]\).

---

### 2. Study the function \(f(x)=|x|^x\)

Define

\[
f(x)=|x|^x,\qquad x\in[-1,1],
\]

with the continuous extension \(f(0)=1\). Indeed,

\[
\ln f(x)=x\ln|x|
\]

and

\[
\lim_{x\to 0} x\ln|x|=0,
\]

so \(f(x)\to 1=f(0)\). Thus \(f\) is continuous on \([-1,1]\).

Now \(a_j=f(\sin j)\), so the cluster points of \(a_j\) are exactly \(f([-1,1])\). Hence

\[
\limsup_{j\to\infty} a_j=\max_{x\in[-1,1]} f(x).
\]

---

### 3. Maximize \(f(x)\) on \([-1,1]\)

For \(0\le x\le 1\),

\[
f(x)=x^x=e^{x\ln x}\le 1,
\]

because \(x\ln x\le 0\).

For \(-1\le x<0\), write \(x=-t\), where \(0<t\le 1\). Then

\[
f(x)=t^{-t}=e^{-t\ln t}.
\]

So we maximize

\[
\phi(t)=-t\ln t
\]

on \((0,1]\). We have

\[
\phi'(t)=-\ln t-1,
\]

so \(\phi'(t)=0\) when \(t=e^{-1}\). Since

\[
\phi''(t)=-\frac1t<0,
\]

this is a maximum. Its value is

\[
\phi(e^{-1})=e^{-1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
f(x)\le e^{1/e},
\]

with equality at

\[
x=-e^{-1}.
\]

---

### 4. Conclude the limsup

Because \(\{\sin j\}\) is dense in \([-1,1]\), there are integers \(j_k\to\infty\) such that

\[
\sin j_k\to -\frac1e.
\]

By continuity of \(f\),

\[
a_{j_k}=f(\sin j_k)\to f\!\left(-\frac1e\right)=e^{1/e}.
\]

Thus

\[
\limsup_{j\to\infty} a_j=e^{1/e}.
\]

\[
\boxed{e^{1/e}}
\]
